newsitem.title: USA: Ranariddh urges indefinite U.S. ban on Cambodia aid.
newsitem.headline: Ranariddh urges indefinite U.S. ban on Cambodia aid.

text.p: Cambodia's Prince Norodom Ranariddh on Friday asked U.S. officials for an indefinite suspension of aid to his country beyond the 30 days already announced in response to the seizure of power by Hun Sen.

Ranariddh was ousted as First Prime Minister on Sunday by his co-prime minister, Hun Sen, after two days of fighting in Phnom Penh. He found deep sympathy for Cambodia's situation from several top U.S. lawmakers.

House of Representatives International Relations Committee chairman Benjamin Gilman had harsh words for the Clinton administration's reaction to the weekend power grab and charged that a weak U.S. response to earlier events in the Southeast Asian kingdom had encouraged Hun Sen.
Gilman, a New York Republican, told Ranariddh: "We are distressed that the suspension was only for 30 days, and the State Department has yet to describe Hun Sen's treachery as a coup."
He offered support to Ranariddh in restoring democracy to the kingdom and said the United States should have taken a stronger stance after a March 30 grenade attack on a Phnom Penh protest rally.

"Regrettably the administration responded tentatively to that act of terrorism, which left 19 innocent people dead ... This only encouraged Hun Sen to believe that he could repress all political opposition and take the country by force," he said at the outset of the panel's meeting with Ranariddh.
"Our committee will do whatever we can to help you in your struggle for democracy," he added.
The senior Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee also urged the administration to condemn Hun Sen's actions as a coup d'etat and welcomed the decision to suspend U.S. aid.

"All such assistance, including loans provided by the World Bank and other international financial institutions, should remain suspended until the democratically elected government of Cambodia is restored," Sen. Joe Biden of New Jersey said.
"I am deeply concerned about the brutal subversion of democracy underway in Cambodia," Biden said. He urged Hun Sen and Ranariddh to settle their differences peacefully in democratic elections.
Ranariddh told reporters he found a "very positive" reception in his meetings with lawmakers. "I think that action will be taken."

"I expressed my relative satisfaction for the stand made by the U.S. administration to freeze aid for 30 days. I think that 30 days is not enough," he said after meeting with members of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee.
In New York on Thursday Ranariddh urged the U.N. Security Council not to recognise any government resulting from the coup and made the same request to that body for a freeze on aid to Cambodia.
Also Thursday the State Department announced the suspension of aid for 30 days, but spokesman Nicholas Burns said after that time programmes that provide humanitarian aid would likely be resumed.
But he added the United States would not resume "those portions of our aid programme that in some way, directly or indirectly, support the government of Cambodia."
The United States allocated $35 million in aid to the Southeast Asian state for fiscal 1997 ending on Oct. 1.
